To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) motor behaviors are a valid and useful tool to understand ASD; (2) motor tests are a good complement for cognitive and social tests; (3) the cerebellum is a good model for motor learning in ASD; (4) cerebellum controlled motor tests are a useful tool to understand cerebellum related motor deficits in ASD.

(1) the most commonly used behavioral mouse models of ASD are based on a limited number of symptoms; (2) these tests do not necessarily provide the best way to study the pathology of ASD in mouse models; (3) motor learning is a good way to study ASD pathology in mouse models; and (4) cerebellum controlled motor learning is an excellent way to study the pathophysiology of ASD in mice.
the cerebellum is involved in ASD pathology, and that motor tests are a useful way to study cerebellum function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and validation of motor learning tests for the assessment of mouse models of ASD.
the development and validation of a behavioral assay that will be able to identify cerebellum mediated deficits in motor learning.
the use of mouse models of ASD to understand the underlying causes of the disease and to develop new treatments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of behavioral tests to assess ASD-like phenotypes in mice is not straightforward, but can be improved by including motor learning tests in the repertoire of behavioral assays.
there is a clear need for the inclusion of cerebellar motor behaviors as a component of the behavioral characterization of ASD mouse models.
the behavioral tests used to study ASD in mice are not sufficient to describe the disorder.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cerebellum plays a role in ASD, and that motor learning tasks are a useful tool to investigate ASD pathology in mouse models.
motor learning is an important aspect of the ASD phenotype and should be included as a behavioral test when assessing mouse models.
behavioral tests for motor learning should be included in the behavioral phenotyping battery of all mouse models of ASD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
motor behaviors can be used as a tool to understand ASD pathology in mice and humans, and can be used to validate the use of a given ASD mouse model.
the cerebellum is an important brain area for ASD research and that the study of motor learning in mouse models of ASD will provide a better understanding of ASD symptoms.
motor behaviors should be included in the behavioral testing of mouse models of ASD, and that the most appropriate motor tasks are the ones that are cerebellum dependent.
